statement: If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.
heath_proof: For let the circles ABC, CDG cut one another at the points B, C; I say that they will not have the same centre. For, if possible, let it be E; let EC be joined, and let EFG be drawn through at random. Then, since the point E is the centre of the circle ABC, EC is equal to EF. [I. Def. 15] Again, since the point E is the centre of the circle CDG, EC is equal to EG. But EC was proved equal to EF also; therefore EF is also equal to EG, the less to the greater: which is impossible. Therefore the point E is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDG.
ai_proof_text:
3.5
**Statement:** If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.

**Step 1.** Let the circles ABC and CDG cut one another at the points B and C. Suppose, if possible, that the two circles have the same centre, and let that common centre be E.

**Step 2.** Join EC (P1). Since the circles ABC and CDG cut one another, they are two distinct circles whose circumferences do not coincide; hence there is a point F on the circumference of circle ABC which does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG.

**Step 3.** Join EF (P1). Since E, being the centre of circle CDG, lies within that circle, the straight line drawn from E through F and, if F falls within circle CDG, produced in a straight line beyond F (P2), passes out of circle CDG and so meets its circumference; let it meet the circumference of circle CDG at the point G, on the same side of E as F. Because F does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the points F and G are distinct. Thus E, F, G lie on one straight line with F and G on the same side of E, so that one of the straight lines EF, EG is a part of the other: if F lies within circle CDG, EF is a part of EG, and if F lies outside circle CDG, EG is a part of EF.

**Step 4.** Since E is the centre of circle ABC (D1.16), and the points C and F both lie on the circumference of circle ABC, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EF (D1.15).

**Step 5.** Since E is also the centre of circle CDG (D1.16), and the points C and G both lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EG (D1.15).

**Step 6.** Therefore EF is equal to EG, since each of them is equal to EC (CN1).

**Step 7.** But by Step 3 one of EF, EG is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5); so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 8.** Therefore E is not the centre of both circles ABC and CDG. Hence, if two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre. Q.E.D.
